preamble: Reduction of unstressed /e/ to schwa [ə]. In English, late Old English unstressed vowels fell together, and by Early Middle English all unstressed vowels were written <e>, representing /ə/. In Old French, pretonic Latin e and ē in an initial open syllable became [ə], as in venīre > venir [vəˈniʁ] and dēbēre > devoir. In Eastern Catalan the reduction is an active stress-conditioned alternation: unstressed /e/ and /ɛ/ are realized as [ə], while Valencian keeps [e].

examples.note: Unstressed vowels merged and were written <e>, representing /ə/, by Early Middle English; final /ə/ was lost around Chaucer's time (Modern 'sun').
Pretonic e in an initial open syllable reduced to [ə], as also seen in Old French deveir [dəˈvei̯ɾ] (below).
Same reduction of the pretonic vowel; the schwa is often dropped in modern informal speech ([dvwaʁ]).
In Eastern Catalan the unstressed vowels /a/, /e/ and /ɛ/ reduce to [ə]; Valencian does not reduce /e/.
